1.pericope_label: The dwelling, and the ten curtains

schools.summary: Gill reads the tabernacle as a type twice over, of Christ's human nature and of the church; Calvin grants that the richness taught how precious the worship of God is, then sets a limit against the whole allegorising method — God did not intend mysteries in every hook and loop, and it is better to confess ignorance than indulge conjecture, the writer to the Hebrews being his model of restraint.

Henry reads the choice of a tent as suited both to a people in the wilderness and to a church that has no continuing city, and warns that church privileges are movable goods and a candlestick in a tent easily taken away.

Clarke pictures Jehovah as a king with his pavilion among his people, distinguishes the loom-work from the needlework, converts the measurements, and asks where such work was done — probably brought from Egypt, looms and all, since the ornamental arts had reached a considerable pitch among both peoples. Wesley joins Henry on the cherubim and on the many churches made one.

Ellicott renders the name literally as 'the dwelling', explains fine twined linen as thread of several strands after the Egyptian manner, and contrasts inwoven patterning with embroidery, noting that inweaving figures was well understood in Egypt.

outliers.claim: no one in his senses will admit that every part of the tabernacle carried a mystical meaning; frivolous conjecture is worse than confessed ignorance

schools.summary: Gill canvasses what the fastenings were called — buttons by some, hooks by others — and settles on clasps.

Ellicott reports Fergusson's demonstration that a twenty-cubit span roofed at a right angle needs a cloth of almost exactly twenty-eight cubits, explains the division into two curtains by portability, flags an anomalous article, corrects 'take hold' to 'correspond', and reads the closing clause as guarding the tabernacle's unity against a roof made in two pieces; Keil and Delitzsch give the sewing and the fifty hyacinth loops, and follow Bähr in concluding that the cloth hung down the walls outside the framework, leaving the gilded beams visible within.

themes: so the dwelling shall be one

7.pericope_label: The goats' hair tent and the outer coverings

schools.summary: Gill describes the material as the finer down of goats spun by women into a stuff like camlet, and leaves open whether the rams' skins covered the whole or only the roof, reporting Jarchi for the roof and preferring the whole.

Henry reads the layering morally and takes care which way it runs — the outside coarse and the beauty within, so that those in whom God dwells must labour to be better than they seem, where hypocrites put the best side outward; he notes that the clasps here were brass where the inner ones were gold, and that the bonds of unity may be as strong between curtains of goats' hair as between purple and scarlet.

Clarke counts four coverings, admits that why there should be four does not appear, and guesses at respect, the desert sand and the heat that would otherwise destroy the woodwork; Wesley will not defend the usual rendering of the outermost skin, preferring some strong but very fine leather.

Keil and Delitzsch note that Bedouin tents are still woven from black goats' hair by the women, and describe the sixth breadth folded double into a kind of gable; Ellicott corrects 'covering' to 'tent', traces the half-breadth left hanging at the back, and argues from the function of keeping out rain that the outer coverings must have reached over the whole dwelling.

15.pericope_label: The boards, the tenons and the silver sockets

schools.summary: Gill calls the boards properly the walls, without which the curtains would be blown about by every wind, and describes the sockets as the foundation of the whole, each a talent of silver from the offering at the numbering of the people.

Henry turns the boards into the figure he wants, a heart established with grace supporting a profession that will not otherwise hold out; he reads the splendour as fitted to the church's infancy and sets against it the gospel builders who had no silver or gold, and notices that no orders are given about the floor.

Clarke asks where sawyers and joiners got their tools, and answers that the Israelites, as the general workmen of Egypt, each carried off the implements of his trade; Wesley repeats Henry's account of the tenons, rings and bars almost word for word.

Keil and Delitzsch decline both extremes on the thickness — not Josephus' four fingers, but still less a cubit, which would make boards no acacia could yield and no desert road could carry — and read the tenons as pegs joined by a dovetailed fastening rather than pegged into one another; Ellicott does the arithmetic of forty sockets for twenty boards.

sides.position: neither — a cubit would make blocks no acacia could yield and no desert road could carry

22.pericope_label: The back, the corner boards, the bars, and the pattern

schools.summary: Gill reports Lightfoot's reconstruction of the corner planks, has the bars keep the boards tight and firm, notes the difficulty that only the middle bar is said to reach from end to end, and observes that plating the boards with gold would take a great quantity and make them heavy, so that some have thought them merely gilt.
Clarke reasons the same way about the gold: how thick it was is not stated, and the plates must have been very thin — something like gold leaf — or the boards would have been insupportably heavy.

Ellicott corrects the compass, the west being 'behind' to Orientals, shows that six boards fall a cubit short of the ten wanted so that the corner boards must make up the difference, counts fifteen bars and distinguishes the middle one, and admits that however minute — even tediously minute — the description, a multitude of particulars could not be put in words and had to come from the pattern Moses saw; Keil and Delitzsch record the coupling of the corner boards into one ring and insist that even the setting up was prescribed.

themes: the middle bar from end to end

31.pericope_label: The veil between the holy and the most holy

schools.summary: Gill offers three readings of what the veil signified and settles on the last — man's sin, or the obscurity of the legal dispensation, or rather the human nature of Christ, the veil of his flesh; Calvin makes the obscurity the principal thing, the veil telling Israel that full revelation had not yet come so that their faith might stretch forward to the Messiah, and adds that two veils together taught them not to break boldly in upon sacred things.

Henry reads the partition through the Epistle to the Hebrews — the way into the holiest was not made manifest while the first tabernacle stood — and draws the consequence that we now enter with boldness, but a boldness obliging reverence and a humble sense of distance.

Clarke argues the typology from the root meaning to rend, so that the veil answered to the body rent upon the cross; and he relays Calmet's objection to the rabbinic four fingers' thickness, since a tabernacle with no window needed no such barrier to sight. Wesley follows Henry closely.

Ellicott makes an inner and an outer sanctuary of the essence of the dwelling; Keil and Delitzsch give the word its sense of division and set the curtain on four gilded pillars in silver sockets, parting the dwelling into ten cubits and twenty.

33.pericope_label: Where the veil hung, and what stood on either side

schools.summary: Gill fixes the veil at the point where the two great pieces of tapestry were clasped together, citing Lightfoot that the division of the curtains answered the division of the house, and reads the mercy seat with its cherubim as a representation of salvation published in the gospel by its ministers.

Ellicott resists letting the arithmetic follow too quickly: if 'under the taches' means directly under them the dwelling divides into equal halves, but the preposition may be vague, and the innermost chamber may have been half the size of the outer as it was in the Temple; Keil and Delitzsch give the proportion as ten cubits and twenty, and set the candlestick opposite the table, one on the south side and one on the north.

debates.question: Were the two chambers of equal size?

sides.position: ten cubits and twenty — the curtain hung where the clasps fell
possibly equal, if 'under the taches' is exact — or half and half as in the Temple, if the word is used loosely

themes: food and light in the outer room
the line the whole chapter makes

schools.summary: Gill accounts for the five pillars as one at each corner of the entrance and three between, leaving four ways for the priests to enter, and explains the plating rather than gilding by the wear of continual passing, the overlay covering the heads and fillets while the wood showed in places.

Clarke orders the three coverings by their distance from the world, this being the first veil and the partition the second, and closes the chapter by reversing its arrangement — under the gospel everything the tabernacle hid is laid open, the way into the holiest made manifest and the awful distance abolished.

Ellicott explains the odd number of pillars by the tent-pole a gable end requires, and makes that fifth pillar the solid basis of Fergusson's tent theory; Keil and Delitzsch deny that the term means embroidery at all, holding it to mean work in stripes or checks — and name the authorities they contradict, including themselves in an earlier book.

debates.question: Does the word describe embroidery or weaving in mixed colours?

sides.position: embroidery with the needle, contrasted with inwoven patterning
neither figures nor needlework but stripes or checks woven in mixed colours — a position Keil adopts against the Rabbins, Gesenius, Bähr and his own earlier book
